### Release Notes

<details>
<summary>jdx/jactionlint (jactionlint)</summary>

### [`v2.6.0`](https://redirect.github.com/jdx/jactionlint/releases/tag/v2.6.0): : `jactionlint update` checks and applies action updates, with optional SHA pinning

[Compare Source](https://redirect.github.com/jdx/jactionlint/compare/v2.5.0...v2.6.0)

jactionlint 2.6.0 adds `jactionlint update`, which finds newer releases of the actions and reusable workflows you use and can pin them to commit SHAs. This release also fixes `jactionlint run --container` for containers whose platform differs from the host, and the action can now download jactionlint with a token so it isn't hit by GitHub's limits on anonymous downloads.

#### Added

##### `jactionlint update`: update actions and pin to SHAs

`jactionlint update` checks the external actions and reusable workflows in your workflows and `action.yml` files. It finds the latest release your policy allows, then lists, previews or writes the new references. It is separate from `--fix`, so a lint run never changes a version. Use it locally, in a hook or as a CI check. Use Dependabot or Renovate if you want pull requests instead. ([#​335](https://redirect.github.com/jdx/jactionlint/issues/335), [@​jdx](https://redirect.github.com/jdx))

```sh
jactionlint update              # list available updates, change nothing
jactionlint update --check      # exit 1 on an update, a policy violation or an unverifiable reference
jactionlint update --diff       # unified diff, change nothing
jactionlint update --apply      # write the changes
```

- **Policy.** Set the policy in a new `update:` section of the config file, or with command-line options, which override the config:
  ```yaml
  # .github/jactionlint.yaml
  update:
    cooldown-days: 7
    freeze: true
    include-tags: "v*"
    exclude-tags: ["*-{alpha,beta,rc}*"]
    exclude-prereleases: true
    require-immutable-releases: true
  ```
  The matching options are `--min-age`, `--freeze`, `--include-tag` and `--exclude-tag`. Other options: `--pin-only` pins the current release without upgrading it, `--branch-to-tag REGEX` converts branch refs such as `@main` to the latest release, `--include-action`/`--exclude-action` filter by action, and `--action-rule REGEX=ignore|cooldown:DAYS` sets a policy for specific actions.
- **Safety.** It never moves a reference to an older version. If a newer release is held back by the cooldown, it says so. Before updating a pinned SHA, it checks the SHA and its version comment against the repository's tags. It edits only the ref and the version in the comment, and keeps quotes, indentation, line endings and comments that are still true. A line it can't edit without guessing is reported and left as is. A failed lookup is reported as `update-unverified` and never counted as up to date.
- **Output.** Findings have the IDs `update-available`, `update-policy`, `update-unverified` and `update-held`, and work with every `--format`, including SARIF. They aren't linter rules, so `--ignore`, `ignores` and ignore comments don't apply to them. Use `--exclude-action`, `--action-rule` or `--changed-since` to leave references out. `update` always uses the online settings (token, cache, GHES, github.com fallback).
- **Actions lock file.** If `.github/workflows/actions.lock` exists, `--apply` ends by running `gh actions-lock --relock` from the repository root, even when no reference changed. The listing, `--check` and `--diff` never run it. If `gh` or the extension is missing, or the relock fails, `update` exits `3`. Workflow edits made before that point stay written. ([#​341](https://redirect.github.com/jdx/jactionlint/issues/341), [@​jdx](https://redirect.github.com/jdx))

See the [update guide](https://redirect.github.com/jdx/jactionlint/blob/main/docs/update.md) for details.

##### Authenticated release downloads

When `JACTIONLINT_TOKEN` is set, `download-jactionlint.bash` sends it with the release download request to github.com. It is never sent to the redirect host. The GitHub Action passes its `token` input to the script, which is `github.token` by default. On GitHub Enterprise Server, the action doesn't pass the token. Without the variable, downloads work without credentials as before. ([#​346](https://redirect.github.com/jdx/jactionlint/issues/346), [@​jdx](https://redirect.github.com/jdx), [@​joschi](https://redirect.github.com/joschi))

#### Fixed

- **`jactionlint run --container`** now uses the container's platform instead of the host's. Before, JavaScript actions (`setup-*`, `actions/github-script`, `jdx/mise-action`) failed with an exec format error when run from a Mac or in a container of another architecture. The platform comes from `--platform`, then `DOCKER_DEFAULT_PLATFORM`, then the image's own platform. Each container platform gets its own tool cache and matching Node.js build, and a `node` on the host's `PATH` is never used inside a container. `runner.os`, `runner.arch`, `RUNNER_OS` and `RUNNER_ARCH` now report the container's platform, so steps under `if: runner.os == 'Linux'` run instead of being skipped. `runner.temp` and `runner.tool_cache`, which were empty before, now match `RUNNER_TEMP` and `RUNNER_TOOL_CACHE`. ([#​344](https://redirect.github.com/jdx/jactionlint/issues/344), [@​jdx](https://redirect.github.com/jdx))
- **`unpinned-tools`** (pedantic) no longer reports `go install tool`, which installs the tools at the versions fixed by `go.mod` and `go.sum`. Bare `all`, `std` and `cmd` are no longer reported either. `go install example.com/x` without a version is still reported. ([#​338](https://redirect.github.com/jdx/jactionlint/issues/338), [@​ktsu2i](https://redirect.github.com/ktsu2i))
- Binaries are now built with Go 1.27.4, which fixes [GO-2026-6859](https://pkg.go.dev/vuln/GO-2026-6859), an `net/http` server crash. ([#​345](https://redirect.github.com/jdx/jactionlint/issues/345), [@​jdx](https://redirect.github.com/jdx))

#### New Contributors

- [@​ktsu2i](https://redirect.github.com/ktsu2i) made their first contribution in [#​338](https://redirect.github.com/jdx/jactionlint/issues/338)
- [@​joschi](https://redirect.github.com/joschi) made their first contribution in [#​346](https://redirect.github.com/jdx/jactionlint/issues/346) (originally [#​342](https://redirect.github.com/jdx/jactionlint/issues/342))

**Full Changelog**: <https://github.com/jdx/jactionlint/compare/v2.5.0...v2.6.0>

content.text:
No — with the current `.github/renovate.json`, dev-tool bumps are **not** automerged. PR #30 says so itself in its body: 🚦 *"Automerge: Disabled by config. Please merge this manually once you are satisfied."*

The config reserves automerge for exactly two categories, both following the principle *"automerge only where green CI provably means correct"*:

| Update type | Automerge? | Why |
|---|---|---|
| apk **pkgrel-only** pin bumps (`1.22-r7 → r8`) | ✅ yes | Alpine rebuild of the same upstream release — CLI unchanged by definition, no review needed |
| Supervisor **schema pin** (`supervisor_ref`) | ✅ yes | Green `validate:apps` against the new ref *proves* the app configs validate |
| apk **pkgver** bumps (minor/major) | ❌ manual (`needs-review`) | CLI semantics may change (e.g. `hd-idle-genargs`) |
| mise `[tools]` pins — **this PR**, jactionlint 2.5→2.6 | ❌ manual | See below |
| hk pair (mise + `hk.pkl`) | ❌ manual | Same weekly Monday cadence, no automerge rule |
| GitHub Actions | ❌ manual | Weekly Monday cadence, no automerge rule |

The `mise` package rule's description says the intent explicitly: the CI check job validates the bumped toolset *before merge*, but the merge itself stays human. That's deliberate — a minor/major tool release can change lint behavior (jactionlint 2.6.0, for instance, adds new checks and an `update` subcommand), so unlike a pkgrel rebuild or a schema-validation pass, "CI green" doesn't fully certify a tool bump harmless. Also note `platformAutomerge: false`, so even where automerge *is* configured it's Renovate doing the merge, not GitHub branch-protection automerge.

**For PR #30 specifically:** it's in good shape to merge by hand right now — all checks are green (including "Mise check (lint + validate)" against the new jactionlint), `MERGEABLE`/`CLEAN`, no conflicts. It arrived from the scheduled Monday-morning Renovate run. If you find yourself manually merging these every week and decide tool bumps *should* auto-merge once CI is green, adding `automerge: true` to the `mise` and hk rules would do it — but as configured today, manual is the expected behavior.
I think I'd like mise tool, hk and GitHub Actions bumps that pass CI to be automerged (Renovate doing the merge is fine). Do we use tools or Github Actions we should by no means auto-bump?

# Loaded Skill: ha-app-workflow (skill)

Change and release discipline for this Home Assistant apps repository – branching, Conventional Commits, lint gates, the single-version-per-branch release rule with changelogs, CI-as-source-of-truth, device-access policy, and the version-sensitive-facts rule. Use before making any change, commit, or release in this repo.

## Content

# Change and release workflow

## Before starting

- Check the current branch first (`git status`): **Always work on a branch named `agent-<topic>`**, create one if needed
  (based off of `main`, i.e. `git switch -c agent-<topic> main`).
- If work belongs on a branch but a stray commit already landed on `main`: move it
  (`git switch -c agent-…; git branch -f main <upstream-tip>`) and disclose it to the user.
- Never stage unrelated WIP: check `git status` before staging and add files explicitly.

## Commits

- Conventional Commits (`build`, `chore:`, `ci`, `docs:`, `feat:`, `fix:`, `perf`, `refactor`, `revert`, `style`,
  `test`); scope app changes (`fix(nfs-server): …`); one commit per logical unit.
- Final trailer line: `Assisted-by: Goose:<model-slug>` – the model name without provider prefix, e.g.
  `Assisted-by: Goose:glm-5.3-flash`.
- The commit-msg hook enforces the format; escape hatch `HK=0 git commit`.

## Before finishing a change

Run `mise run check` – lint plus validate; it is the same gate CI runs. Lint-stack details and scoped checking: skill
`ha-app-tooling`. Task usage: `mise run check --help`.

## App releases

- A working branch starting from `main` bumps `version` in `config.yaml` to a **single** next version (major, minor or
  patch by semantic versioning): the branch ships one version, not one per commit, and continuously expands that
  version's `CHANGELOG.md` entry until it lands on `main`.
- Transitory extra versions within the branch are fine where testing demands one (AppArmor profile changes are only
  re-applied on app *update*, never on rebuild) – squash them back into the single version (config plus one merged
  changelog entry) before merging.
- CI enforces the rule: `.github/workflows/version-guard.yaml` fails when device-visible app files (`rootfs/`,
  `Dockerfile`, `config.yaml`, `apparmor.txt`, `translations/`) changed without a version bump – the Supervisor's update
  model makes a no-bump change a silent no-op that only repoints an already-published version tag. Exception: if the
  base version's GHCR tag was never published (its release's build/publish failed), the guard probes GHCR and passes –
  reusing the version then repoints nothing; unprovable fails closed. Changes to docs-only files (README, DOCS,
  CHANGELOG, KNOWLEDGE, TODO, `.agents/`), the per-app `.dockerignore` (it shapes the build context but never changes
  the image the device receives), and repo tooling do not require a version bump.

## CI/CD is the source of truth for what gets published

- Pushes to `main` build and publish images (`.github/workflows/builder.yaml`). If CI fails, fix the repo, not CI config
  – unless the CI config itself is wrong.
- Builder caveats: the init job needs `fetch-depth: 0` – the changed-files filter otherwise only sees the tip commit and
  silently skips multi-commit merges, so use regular merges instead of squash merges.
- The app `Dockerfile` must not pull from Docker Hub at build time (rule and rationale: skill `ha-app-scaffolding`).
- The lint workflow runs frenck's app linter natively (pinned source plus pypi requirements), not via its Docker action
  (whose Docker Hub image builds flaked with 504s and 429 runner-pool rate limits).
- In `.github/workflows/`, match GitHub users and bots by immutable user id, never by `login` (root `KNOWLEDGE.md`
  §"GitHub Actions: user identity matching").

## Device access

Testing against the real HA device over SSH only on explicit user request; otherwise hand the user exact commands to
run. On-device procedures: skill `ha-app-device-testing`.

## Version-sensitive facts

Supervisor schemas, s6-overlay layout, HAOS kernel configs and HA docs change frequently. Wherever such facts are
written down (`KNOWLEDGE.md`, comments, skills), cite the source (URL plus version/ref). Before relying on them for new
work, re-verify against the latest docs/source.

## Design change proposals

When a fix reveals a design issue, diagnose hands-on first (strace, packet captures, a reproduction lab), then explain
root cause, options and trade-offs to the user before rewriting.

## Text files

Every text file ends with a final newline (the lint gate enforces it).

# Loaded Skill: ha-app-tooling (skill)

How this repository's dev tooling works – the hk lint gate and git hooks, mise task authoring with usage specs, what the validate tasks check, and the YAML/shell/TOML linting conventions. Use when touching hk.pkl, mise tasks, or lint configuration, or when interpreting lint failures.

## Content

# Dev tooling (hk, mise tasks, validation, linting)

**Task usage is not documented here**: `mise run <task> --help` is the authoritative, always-current usage for every
task (args, flags, choices). This skill covers only the conventions and gotchas behind the tasks.

## Lint gate (hk)

- `mise run check` – lint plus validate; **always run before finishing a change**. CI's `check` job and `mise run lint`
  run `hk check --all` over every tracked file; plain `hk check` lints only modified files (fast local feedback).
  Untracked files are never selected (verified for hk 2.7.1, `check` and `--all` alike, independent of HK_STASH
  settings); `HK_MISE=1` lets hk resolve mise environments in hooks and `HK_STASH_UNTRACKED=0` additionally keeps
  untracked worktree files out of the pre-commit stash/restore cycle and skips their discovery (both set in
  `mise.toml`).
- To check an explicit file set, pipe NUL-separated paths to hk:
  `git diff --name-only -z HEAD | hk check --files0-from=-`.
- Pkl interpolates strings with `\(expr)` – a `${expr}` sequence inside a string is literal text. Globs built by
  interpolation (e.g. `hk.pkl`'s `vendoredExcludes` map) must use `\(…)`: the `${…}` form silently matches nothing
  (verified against hk 2.12.0).
- Git hooks (enable once per machine: `mise run install-git-hooks`, after `mise install --locked`; needs Git 2.54+,
  installs user-wide, silently no-ops in repos without `hk.pkl`): pre-commit auto-fixes (panache format, tombi format,
  ryl format, final newlines, shfmt, dockerfmt, shellcheck autofixes) and gates the commit; commit-msg enforces
  Conventional Commits. Escape hatch: `HK=0 git commit`.
- `mise.toml`'s `[[watch_files]]` entry auto-runs `hk fix` on the files you touched whenever a mise-activated shell
  redisplays its prompt (skipped when git just rewrote them from commits, e.g. checkout/pull). Its `patterns` mirror
  hk.pkl's fix-step selections – keep the two in sync when changing either side.

## mise task authoring

- File tasks live in `.mise/tasks/` with proper suffixes (`.sh`, `.py`, … – mise resolves the short names, e.g.
  `mise run lint`) and `#MISE`/`#USAGE` header comments.
- Document and type task arguments via usage specs – never bare `$1` handling unless `raw_args = true`.
- Required args: declare `arg "<name>"` – mise errors before the task starts when missing (no manual checks). Read
  required string args with `${usage_name:?}` – it also rejects empty values, which pass mise's presence check (mise
  docs, "Read argument values": `?` errors only when unset, `:?` also when empty). Optional args read with
  `${usage_name:-…}` (empty ≡ unset); boolean flags with `${usage_name:-false}`, compared against `"true"`. In Python
  tasks the values are exported as `usage_<underscored_name>` env vars – reject empty required values explicitly there
  (the `:?` guard is shell-only).

## validate:apps (`.mise/tasks/validate/apps.py`, part of `mise run check`)

- Fetches supervisor schemas from the ref pinned in `mise.toml` `[vars].supervisor_ref` (cached under `~/.cache/`).
- Renovate bumps that pin to the newest supervisor release and automerges the bump once CI `check` is green (rebase
  merge strategy, `.github/renovate.json`) – green means the new schemas validate our app configs. Renovate does not
  track schema-*behavior* changes: re-verify version-sensitive supervisor facts against the new ref before relying on
  them (skill `ha-app-workflow`).
- apk pin drift is a separate task: `mise run validate:apk-pins` (`.mise/tasks/validate/apk-pins.py`) compares pinned
  apk package versions in app Dockerfiles against the Alpine binary indexes (drift = guided release – root
  `KNOWLEDGE.md` §"apk package version policy"); CI runs it only on main pushes and the daily cron (lint workflow),
  never in the PR gate – the indexes are Alpine's publishing state, not the PR's. TOML config schemas are validated by
  the hk `tombi-lint` step instead (section below); `.github/renovate.json` is gated by the official
  renovate-config-validator hk step (see the linting section below).

## YAML linting: ryl

- YAML is linted by ryl (hk `ryl-lint` step, config `.ryl.toml`, pinned as `aqua:owenlamont/ryl` in mise.toml).
- ryl parses YAML 1.2; yamllint defaulted to 1.1: bareword booleans (`yes`/`no`/`on`/`off`, any case) are plain strings
  and leading-zero integers like `0755` are decimal – while YAML 1.1 parsers (PyYAML and kin) still coerce both. Do not
  predict what a parser will load from ryl's lint view.
- The hk step runs `ryl check --strict` (`--strict` added to both `check` and `fix`): warning-level rules fail the gate
  like errors (warning-only runs exit `2`, errors `1`).
- The builtin's `check_diff` wiring is cleared (`check_diff = null`, `check_after_diff = false`): ryl's `--diff` exit
  code only reflects patch presence – it exits `0` whenever nothing is fixable, including files with unfixable warnings
  or errors – and hk's fix mode skips the fixer when `check_diff` exits `0`, so violating files would pass pre-commit
  untouched. With `check_diff` gone, fix mode runs `fix` (carrying `--strict`) on every staged YAML file and its exit
  code decides: `0` only when nothing remains to fix or flag. (Upstream issue: root `TODO.md`.)
- YAML is also formatted by `ryl format` (hk `ryl-format` step; also in `mise run fmt`), sharing `.ryl.toml` selection
  and exclusions; its fixes supersede the lint fixer's, so the two pre-commit steps converge in either order (probed ryl
  0.29.0).
- `.ryl.toml` has no `extends`, so it inlines the `default` preset (ryl enables no rules by default) with this repo's
  overrides applied. The override whys: `line-length` at 140/warning because app config descriptions/translations use
  long lines intentionally and Renovate pins action refs to full commit SHAs with a version comment (single-line by YAML
  grammar, impossible to wrap); `truthy.check-keys = false` because GitHub Actions workflows key their triggers on
  `on:`; `document-start` off because HA app files use no leading `---`; `.mise/locks/**` excluded (machine-generated
  minified aube blobs with unwrappable URLs, not prose to lint).
- Config is TOML with `[lint.rules]` (`[rules]` is deprecated as of ryl 0.26). A rule with an option table must not also
  appear as a `"<name>" = "enable"` string in the same table – TOML duplicate key, ryl exits `2` loudly.

## TOML linting: tombi

- TOML is linted and formatted by tombi (hk builtins `tombi`/`tombi_format`, pinned as `tombi` in mise.toml);
  `mise run fmt` formats via `tombi format .`. The lint step adds `--error-on-warnings`: tombi exits 0 when only its
  warn-severity rules fire, and the gate must fail on them (its three built-ins – key-empty, dotted-keys-out-of-order,
  tables-out-of-order – are all warn-severity).
- Schemas bind per-file via a `#:schema <url>` top directive (Taplo-compatible; must be the document's first comment,
  followed by a blank line). Renovate auto-bumps our tools, so "latest" is usually the right schema ref. The repo-level
  `.tombi.toml` config file defines the TOML formatting rules (only deviations from tombi's defaults,
  <https://tombi-toml.github.io/tombi/docs/configuration>).
- tombi validates in **strict mode** (default): objects without `additionalProperties` are treated as closed, so unknown
  keys are errors even when the schema doesn't mark them so – stricter than the stock-JSON-Schema validation
  `validate:apps` performs on the supervisor schemas. Adding a config key the upstream schema doesn't know yet fails the
  gate until the schema learns it: the schema is the contract. Schema deprecations are warn-severity, hence gate-failing
  too.
- Schemas are fetched remotely and cached (`~/.cache/tombi`, 24 h TTL; `tombi cache clean`). Offline runs reuse cached
  copies and silently skip un-cached schemas, while CI always runs online – schema checks therefore track upstream
  main/latest, not the installed tool version, and an upstream schema change can fail the gate with no local change
  (signal, like zizmor's online audits).
- Formatter defaults match .editorconfig; an unformatted file fails the format check.

## Python linting: ruff

- Python (the `.mise/tasks/` scripts) is linted and formatted by ruff via the hk builtins `ruff` (check/fix =
  `ruff check`; the fix path preflights with the builtin's `check_diff`) and `ruff_format` (check via
  `ruff format --diff`, fix via `ruff format`), pinned as `aqua:astral-sh/ruff` in mise.toml. The formatter step runs
  before the linter step; `mise run fmt` runs `ruff format .`.
- Config is `.ruff.toml` (TOML, `#:schema`-bound): the selection is `extend-select` over ruff's default rule set, so the
  gate tracks the canonical upstream defaults (ruff 0.17.0 expanded them and they keep drifting with releases,
  astral-sh/ruff#28786). Accepted trade-off: a ruff release that reshuffles the defaults can newly fire rules and break
  the gate with no repo change (Renovate bumps ruff regularly) – treat that as a review prompt for the new findings,
  then fix them or noqa with a reason. Entries the defaults already carry stay listed as drift insurance.
  `target-version` stays unpinned: nothing couples it to the `python` mise.toml pin, so a pin would drift (ruff's own
  default applies). Note that UP is target-sensitive in the other direction: once ruff's default target crosses py314,
  its safe autofix will drop the no-longer-needed `from __future__ import annotations` imports.
- Never add formatter-conflicting rules (COM812, ISC001, Q000/Q003, W191) – the formatter and linter would fight. The
  security/exception families are deliberately narrow: S307 marks the deliberate `eval()` sites (the `# noqa: S307`
  comments in `validate/apps.py` go live with it); S603/S607/S310 keep the subprocess and URL surfaces audited (inline
  noqa with a reason where intentional); EM + TRY police exception messages, PTH pushes pathlib idioms.
- Type checking runs via the hk builtin `ty` (pinned as `ty` in mise.toml, config `ty.toml`, `#:schema`-bound) after
  ruff: `ty check` over `**/*.py`/`**/*.pyi`. The scripts have no repo-managed Python environment – stdlib-only scripts
  run on the mise python, `validate/apps.py` runs under `uv run --with voluptuous --with pyyaml` – so ty cannot resolve
  third-party imports; suppress those inline (`# ty: ignore[import-not-found] - reason`), never by disabling the rule in
  config (the comment form keeps other same-line diagnostics live, and a config-wide ignore would pass a typo'd import
  anywhere).
- Docstrings (D, google convention) and annotations (ANN) are committed regimes: a docstring's first line is the summary
  (ends with a period), then a blank line before the body, and parameter names must appear in the text (ruff's D417
  checks name presence, not section structure). Every function gets full annotations; dynamic dicts (lab-option
  fixtures) are `dict[str, object]` – never explicit `Any` (ANN401).
- ruff does not read `.editorconfig`; its formatter defaults match this repo's Python style. E501 is the outer fence at
  120 columns (`.ruff.toml` `[lint.pycodestyle]`, panache's prose width) for what the formatter cannot split. Both
  builtins pass `--force-exclude`, so config excludes apply even to hk's explicit file arguments, and ruff resolves the
  config by walking up from each target file – the root `.ruff.toml` covers every task script.
- The `#MISE`/`#USAGE` task directives sit inside `# fmt: off`/`# fmt: on` markers in every task script: ruff format
  normalizes `#MISE` comment spacing (no comment-prefix exclusion exists) and must not touch them. mise's parser
  tolerates the spaced form (its prefix regexes match with `\s*` tolerance, unlike the usage crate's strict `#USAGE`
  regex; mise `src/task/mod.rs`, verified 2026-11-12 against mise 2026.11.6), but the unspaced directives stay canonical
  – keep the markers around the block, and never append anything to directive lines (the header parses as TOML).

## Shell linting

- shfmt (formatting; follows .editorconfig) and shellharden (quoting hardening) are hk *fix* steps – let pre-commit fix
  or run `hk check --fix` instead of hand-formatting; shellcheck `-x` is the lint gate.
- The hk `editorconfig_checker` step runs with `-disable-indent-size`: padding here is marker/string-driven (Markdown
  list indents, quoted-string continuations), so the indent_size-multiple rule is noise – shell indentation is the shfmt
  step's job (.editorconfig). Every other EditorConfig rule stays in force.
- The shfmt style (binary-next-line, indented case) is pinned under `.editorconfig`'s `[**]`, whose `root = true` stops
  EditorConfig discovery at the repo – without it a home-directory config silently defines the style locally and CI sees
  shfmt defaults instead.
- shellharden quotes command substitutions even where word splitting is required (for-loop iterables) – write such loops
  as brace expansion (`for _ in {1..N}`) or arrays (`read -r -a` / `mapfile`) instead. It also quotes command-string
  executions (`if "$NFSD_CMD"`) where quoting changes what is *executed*: the whole string becomes one literal command
  name (`command not found` – this broke nfs-server 0.6.1 on-device). Build such commands as arrays
  (`NFSD_CMD=(...); "${NFSD_CMD[@]}"`) so quoting is stable either way. Its parser also loses sync on nested parentheses
  inside arithmetic expansion (`"$(( (a << 8) | b ))"` reports "the parser got lost" on a syntactically complete file
  and mangles everything after it – spurious `""` prefixes, quotes inserted into single-quoted strings); keep arithmetic
  flat, flat `$(( 10#$a ))` is fine – and even flat, avoid `<<` in arithmetic (lexed as a heredoc delimiter, same loss
  of sync; write it out: `$((5 * 2 ** attempt))`). (Upstream items: root `TODO.md`.)

## Workflow, Dockerfile and Renovate config linting

- GitHub workflows, composite actions and Dependabot config: jactionlint (hk builtin; the maintained actionlint fork,
  <https://jactionlint.jdx.dev/>) plus zizmor's security audits. jactionlint auto-reads `.github/jactionlint.yaml` –
  profile `default` = actionlint's correctness checks plus the zizmor-parity regular-persona rules (`pedantic` adds
  auditor-persona noise); it replicates every zizmor audit as a same-ID rule, so the gate runs both deliberately: zizmor
  keeps what jactionlint lacks (confidence grading, pre-commit/repo-slug auditing, LSP mode, its own zizmor.yml config)
  and jactionlint's parity target lags zizmor releases. Its `unpinned-uses` policy and `.github/zizmor.yml` mirror
  `.github/renovate.json`: `home-assistant/*` may float on a branch (the home-assistant org's actions), everything else
  must be digest-pinned – keep all three in sync when adding actions.
- The hk `zizmor` step runs `zizmor -qq --no-progress`; `-qq` trims zizmor's tracing noise (version banner, per-file
  completion notices, the offline-mode notice and the YAML-anchors beta notice – anchors are used by design). Findings
  render regardless of verbosity, so the gate's verdict is unaffected. Its mode follows the environment: a
  `GH_TOKEN`/`GITHUB_TOKEN`/ `ZIZMOR_GITHUB_TOKEN` enables zizmor's four online-only audits (impostor-commit,
  known-vulnerable-actions, ref-confusion, stale-action-refs), without one the audit is fully offline. CI passes its
  default `GITHUB_TOKEN` for the strongest audit; locally the gate stays offline unless a token is exported (opt out
  with `ZIZMOR_NO_ONLINE_AUDITS=1`). Online results depend on remote state: a once-green run can go red when, e.g., a
  security advisory lands for a pinned action – that is signal; re-run or fix forward. zizmor caches API responses
  (~/.cache/zizmor), so a local run shortly after another can reuse them. A finding that must stay (a checkout whose
  later step pushes, e.g. apk-bump's changelog job) carries an inline `# zizmor: ignore[<audit-id>]` comment stating the
  reason.
- Local `uses:` references use GitHub's self-repository syntax (`$/.github/workflows/…`), not `./`: `$/` resolves the
  reference from the running commit by construction, so it counts as digest-pinned (zizmor `self-repository` audit;
  needs runner 2.336.0+).
- Dockerfiles: droast (hadolint-compatible CLI, <https://github.com/immanuwell/dockerfile-roast>; hk builtin) with
  project-level skips in `droast.toml` (DF020/DF036 – the HA base image provides the runtime identity and init via
  s6-overlay). Rule IDs are `DF0xx`; a `# hadolint ignore=DLxxx` pragma is dead weight under droast – inline ignores are
  `# droast ignore=DFxxx reason="…"`, and `droast --hadolint-compatible --hadolint-compatibility-report` maps old DL IDs
  to their DF equivalents. Formatting: dockerfmt (<https://github.com/reteps/dockerfmt>; hk custom step), reading its
  style from `.editorconfig`.
- `.github/renovate.json` is validated by the official `renovate-config-validator` via a custom hk step
  (`--no-global --strict`). `--no-global` matters: bare file args are otherwise validated as a GLOBAL self-hosted
  config, which a repo config is not. `--strict` also fails while the installed Renovate flags a pending config
  migration, so Renovate bumps that deprecate config keys surface immediately.
- Renovate also manages the mise.toml `[tools]` pins (manager `mise`; weekly, Monday, like the other managers) and keeps
  `mise.lock` in sync – including `hk`: a custom regex manager (`.github/renovate.json`) rewrites the `hk@X.Y.Z` package
  imports in `hk.pkl` with the same depName/datasource/currentValue as the mise manager's hk dep, so both land in one
  branch and one PR bumps all three files. Manual bumps use `mise run bump-hk <version>`; the CI check catches partial
  desyncs (`mise install --locked` errors on a mise.toml/mise.lock disagreement). The `npm:renovate` pin carries two
  aube-policy exemptions (mise.toml): `trust_policy_excludes` for `@yarnpkg/libzip` (3.2.2 lost npm provenance vs 3.2.1
  – its release branch lacked `npmPublishProvenance: true`, yarnpkg/berry#7182; aube otherwise blocks the tool tree) and
  `allow_builds` for `re2` (renovate's optional regex accelerator; its install script downloads a prebuilt native binary
  that aube's default-deny lifecycle policy would skip, leaving the module absent and renovate logging a verbose
  RegExp-fallback stack trace on every gate run).

## bashio shebang note

Scripts with the `#!/usr/bin/with-contenv bashio` shebang are plain bash, but hk's shebang-based file typing does not
recognize the wrapper (root `TODO.md`), so `hk.pkl` re-declares each shell builtin's `match_any` with added glob
selectors for the s6 script paths and the apps' `/usr/bin` scripts – keep those globs when adding app scripts.

## Pin digests The `pinDigests` option configures Renovate to add digests to image references that don’t contain them. The following example Renovate configuration includes this option: ```json { "$schema": "https://docs.renovatebot.com/renovate-schema.json", "extends": [ "config:recommended" ], "packageRules": [ { "matchDatasources": ["docker"], "pinDigests": true } ] } ``` This configures Renovate to open pull requests that pin a reference like `cgr.dev/chainguard/python:3.12` to a digest like the following: ``` cgr.dev/chainguard/python:3.12@sha256:e3b524a97c37c32ba590aae0ebcebe3a983c1f69a5093b670fdba980f97a09b3 ``` You can also use the `matchUpdateTypes` option to disable updates for any types other than `digest`. Here is an example Renovate configuration that does this: ```json { "$schema": "https://docs.renovatebot.com/renovate-schema.json", "extends": [ "config:recommended" ], "packageRules": [ { "matchDatasources": ["docker"], "matchUpdateTypes": [ "major", "minor", "patch" ], "enabled": false } ] } ``` This configures Renovate to update the digest for a reference but not the tag. The benefit of this approach is that it lets you define your update strategy for each image reference through a mutable tag, rather than having separate rules for different images in your Renovate configuration, similar to Chainguard’s [Digestabot](https://github.com/chainguard-dev/digestabot) GitHub Action.
[...]
Configure Renovate with the following example, adjusting the `flux.fileMatch` patterns to cover your repository layout. The `pinDigests` rule enforces the [recommended practice of pinning charts to a digest](https://chainguard.dev/docs/chainguard/containers/using-and-deploying/helm-charts/use-chainguard-helm-charts#pin-to-digest): if an `OCIRepository` has a `tag` but no `digest`, Renovate opens a pull request to add one.
[...]
You can use [`renovatebot/github-action`](https://github.com/renovatebot/github-action) to run Renovate from a GitHub Actions workflow. This can be combined with an [assumable identity](https://chainguard.dev/docs/platform/administration/assumable-ids/assumable-ids) to authenticate to `cgr.dev` and update references to Chainguard container images in your repository.

Title: Reconstructing the TJ Actions Changed Files GitHub Actions Compromise
URL: https://snyk.io/blog/reconstructing-tj-actions-changed-files-github-actions-compromise
Published: 2025-03-17
Acquired: 2026-11-14
Snippets:
In the afternoon on Friday, March 14, 2025, details began to emerge about a serious security exploit on a popular GitHub Action called [changed files](https://github.com/tj-actions/changed-files) (*tj-actions/changed-files*). About 23,000 GitHub repos use this Action as part of their CI and DevOps workflows. It allows you to track which files have changed across branches and commits. An attacker with write privileges on the Action repo made a commit that caused encrypted secrets to appear in plaintext in the GitHub Action logs. This could lead to a devastating breach on a public repo where the Action logs are also public.
[...]
As of this writing, it’s unknown why the attacker had write permissions on the repo that houses this GitHub Action code. But, the key enabling factors for this attack beyond just having write permissions were as follows: - Changing existing release tags to point to the attack commit - Having the attack commit orphaned from any branches, including the main branch These factors added a bit of obfuscation to hide the attack. The attack relied on making an external network call to pull down the attack code, which ultimately led to it being noticed by services that monitor anomalous network activity.
[...]
The critical bit is the very last line, where a particular tag of the GitHub Action repo is referenced. The attacker deleted the original version tags and relocated them to the malicious commit, which was the orphaned commit. The attacker re-pointed several existing release tags to their malicious commit, thereby deepening the attack's impact.
[...]
The attacker altered TJ’s `changed-files` GitHub Action to download a script from a remote location, save it to a local file on the virtual machine the GitHub Action was running on, and then execute that script. This was accomplished in two steps. The first step was the malicious, orphaned commit, which has since been deleted.
[...]
A post on Hacker News (found [here](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=43367987#43372246)) that dropped on March 14 indicated that the exploit had been caught by [StepSecurity](https://www.stepsecurity.io/), a service that monitors unauthorized network calls in GitHub Actions (among other things). The author and maintainer of the popular GitHub Action added a comment on that post outlining what happened. The very first issue he identifies is that the attacker had write access to the repo. Because of the swift discovery of the exploit and the responsiveness of the maintainer, the exploit was addressed and shut down very quickly. However, users of the `changed-files` GitHub Action are advised to review their logs since March 14 to ensure no secrets have been leaked to a public Actions log.
[...]
There are a few ways that this particular exploit could have been avoided. 1. For custom, remote GitHub Actions, reference the commit hash directly For instance, you could have: This references the commit hash directly rather than a tag. This is not common practice but would guarantee that the version of the custom GitHub Action that’s run is the version you expect. 2. Use additional custom GitHub Actions to flag unexpected network calls. This is how StepSecurity became aware of the exploit.

We discovered the first steps that appear to have been taken in this multi-layered attack flow. The attackers obtained initial access by taking advantage of the GitHub Actions workflow of SpotBugs, a popular open-source tool for static analysis of bugs in code. This enabled the attackers to move laterally between SpotBugs repositories, until obtaining access to reviewdog.
[...]
**Update March 20:** The recent compromise of the GitHub action tj-actions/changed-files and additional actions within the reviewdog organization has captured the attention of the GitHub community, marking another major software supply chain attack. Our team conducted an in-depth investigation into this incident and uncovered many more details about how the attack occurred and its timeline. These attackers compromised continuous integration/continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipelines of thousands of repositories, putting them at risk. Our team also discovered that the initial attack targeted Coinbase. The payload was focused on exploiting the public CI/CD flow of one of their open source projects (agentkit) probably with the purpose of leveraging it for further compromises. However, the attacker was not able to use Coinbase secrets or publish packages. After this initial attack, we believe the same actor moved on to the larger attack that has since gained widespread attention globally. Our investigations also reveal that the attacker began preparing several days before reports surfaced, eventually affecting specific versions of tj-actions/changed-files and putting a significant number of repositories at risk. This incident underscores how attackers can abuse third-party actions or dependencies to compromise software supply chains, potentially resulting in unauthorized access, data breaches and code tampering.
[...]
The tj-actions/changed-files GitHub action was recently compromised, allowing attackers to access sensitive workflow secrets that relied on this action. This GitHub action was used by over 23,000 GitHub repositories. The compromise was first identified on March 14, 2025, when security researchers [detected suspicious activity](https://github.com/tj-actions/changed-files/issues/2463) made by the action. The attackers injected a payload that dumped the CI/CD runner’s memory, exposing sensitive environment variables and secrets directly to the workflow logs. A [lead provided by Adnan Khan](https://x.com/adnanthekhan/status/1901248035830542619) suggested that the compromise of the tj-actions/changed-files action originated in the compromise of a repository belonging to another GitHub organization: reviewdog/action-setup. We can now confirm that tj-actions/changed-files was compromised because it used the tj-actions/eslint-changed-files action, which relied on reviewdog/action-setup as a dependency. Further investigation revealed that additional actions belonging to the reviewdog organization were hijacked as well. By March 20, the maintainers of both tj-actions and [reviewdog](https://github.com/reviewdog/reviewdog/issues/2079) had applied the necessary security measures, and mitigated the threat.
[...]
Somewhere between March 10 and March 14, 2025, an attacker successfully pushed a malicious commit to the tj-actions/changed-files GitHub repository. This commit contained a Base64-encoded payload shown in Figure 1, which prints all of the credentials that were present in the CI runner’s memory to the workflow’s log. The attacker was able to add the malicious commit ([0e58ed8](https://github.com/tj-actions/changed-files/commit/0e58ed8671d6b60d0890c21b07f8835ace038e67)) to the repository by using a GitHub token with write permissions that they obtained previously. The attacker disguised the commit to look as if it was created by renovate[bot] — a legitimate user. The commit was then added to a legitimate pull request that was opened by the real renovate[bot] and automatically merged, as configured for this workflow. These steps enabled the attacker to infect the repository, without the activity being detected. Once the commit was merged, the attacker pushed new git tags to the repository to override its existing tags, making them all point to the malicious commit in the repository. From that point of compromise, the attacker impacted **every GitHub workflow run that depended on the tj-actions/changed-files action**. On March 14, 2025, the attack on tj-actions/changed-files [was detected by StepSecurity’s researchers](https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/harden-runner-detection-tj-actions-changed-files-action-is-compromised), who reported the incident to the maintainers of the tj-actions organization. As soon as details of the incident were published, the GitHub community started patching workflows and repositories to mitigate the attack. On March 16, [Adnan Khan](https://x.com/adnanthekhan/status/1901248035830542619) shared his research, pointing to the compromise of another GitHub organization — reviewdog. Adnan hypothesized that in the original compromise, the attacker leveraged a workflow configured in the tj-actions/changed-files repository that was using another action belonging to the same organization: tj-actions/eslint-changed-files. In turn, the tj-actions/eslint-changed-files action directly depended on the reviewdog/action-setup action, and used it in its runtime as a composite action. This implied that consumers of the tj-actions/eslint-changed-files action were compromised once it ran, as this action automatically executed the malicious code residing in the compromised reviewdog/action-setup action. When the tj-actions/eslint-changed-files action was executed, the tj-actions/changed-files CI runner’s secrets were leaked, allowing the attackers to steal the credentials used in the runner, including a Personal Access Token (PAT) belonging to the tj-bot-actions GitHub user account.

The attacker then used the token to impersonate the bot and retag all versions of the Action to point to a malicious commit containing a Base64 encoded version of the following script: ![Malicious script injected into tj-actions/changed-files](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/6a8416650513bd2753e8047d/6ab68056033639dfeaf93b6f_Screenshot%25202025-03-18%2520at%25209.47.39%2520AM.png) This code accesses and runs the 'memdump.py' script, finds secrets values within the results, and prints them to the workflow logs, encoding them twice in Base64 to avoid automated detection. ## **Who is at risk?** Any repo with workflows using the ‘tj-actions/changed-files' Action is at risk of a secrets leak. Maintainers of these repos should immediately check the build logs of runs in the above-stated time frame and consider any printed credential compromised. While this is naturally a greater risk for open-source projects, as anyone could have gained access to leaked credentials, maintainers of private projects should still be wary. Any actor with read access to build logs, such as external collaborators or contractors, may have been able to compromise these credentials, even if they do not regularly have access to secrets values. **We strongly recommend rotating secrets used in affected repositories.** ## **How to avoid a similar attack going forward** To mitigate the risk of being affected by this type of attack in the future, always reference specific commit SHAs when using GitHub Actions, as opposed to tags and mutable references (such as @latest or @v1.0.5).

All seven open PRs are green (the one "skipping" is the build matrix, which intentionally doesn't run on PRs). Here's the full picture.

## Do we use anything that should never be auto-bumped?

Yes — one hard no, one conditional no, and a class boundary:

**By no means: `tj-actions/changed-files`** (used in `builder.yaml`'s init job). Its March 2025 compromise (CVE‑2025‑30066) repointed *existing tags* to a malicious commit **without any release** — the payload dumped runner secrets into public logs across ~23k repos, and the attacker even impersonated `renovate[bot]` to land it via automerge in the action's own repo. Our copy is digest-pinned, which is the right mitigation — but automerging its updates would erode it, because green CI proves nothing about an action's integrity: the payload executed *without failing the run*. Notably, the digest-typed update a tag-repoint produces is exactly the artifact a human should see.

**Fails your own criterion ("bumps that pass CI"): the main-branch-only build/publish actions** — `home-assistant/builder/*` and `nick-fields/retry` inside `build-app.yaml`. They never execute in PR CI (only lint + validate run there), so a green PR certifies nothing about them; an automerged bump would land unexecuted on the release path. (Right now this is theoretical: I verified `2026.09.0` is still the newest builder release, so Renovate has nothing to PR yet.)

**What "passing CI" genuinely certifies** — and that's most of your list: the PR gate installs the bumped toolset and runs `hk check --all` + `validate:apps` *with it*, so a green tool bump means the new tools accept the repo as-is, and post-merge PRs run the same gate — nothing slips through. Every PR also exercises `actions/checkout` and `jdx/mise-action` themselves, so those are certified too.

## What I changed

Four rules appended to `.github/renovate.json` (commit `769bce8` on branch `agent-renovate-automerge`, config validated by `renovate-config-validator --strict`, full `mise run check` green):

| Scope | Automerge |
|---|---|
| mise `[tools]` minor/patch (incl. `npm:renovate` 44.x) | ✅ rebase, on green |
| hk pair (mise.toml + mise.lock + hk.pkl in one PR) minor/patch | ✅ rebase, on green |
| `actions/checkout`, `jdx/mise-action` minor/patch | ✅ rebase, on green |
| **All majors** (hk 3.x → hk.pkl contract, renovate 45 config semantics, node/python/go runtime majors, action input changes) | ❌ manual |
| **Digest-typed action updates** (ref repointed, no release) — *all* actions | ❌ manual |
| `tj-actions/changed-files` — unconditionally | ❌ explicit `automerge: false` |
| `home-assistant/builder`, `nick-fields/retry` | ❌ manual (not PR-CI-exercised) |

I kept majors manual deliberately — they're where "green today, breaks tomorrow" lives — but that's one line to flip if you want them in. The digest-only carve-out isn't a limitation in practice: release bumps arrive semver-typed with the digest folded in (verified in Renovate's `lookup` source, and consistent with PR #29), so normal updates still auto-merge; only the no-release-repoint case stays human. Untracked oddities need nothing: `gh = "latest"` and the `go:`-built `entire-agent-goose` pseudo-version never get PRs, and the floating `home-assistant/*` refs are pinless by design across renovate.json/jactionlint.yaml/zizmor.yml.

**Net effect once this lands on main:** the seven open minor/patch PRs (#25 ruff, #26 rumdl, #27 ty, #28 uv, #29 mise‑action, #30 jactionlint, #31 renovate) are all green today — Renovate's next run should merge the whole queue by itself, no clicks. Since there's no branch protection, Renovate does the merging via API (rebase strategy), same as your existing supervisor/apk rules.

input.prompt: Explain the minimumReleaseAge option: (1) exact mechanics — does it withhold/skip creating the update or PR entirely, or block automerge with a pending status check like renovate/stability-days? (2) what happens for updates that have no release timestamp (e.g. digest updates, pinDigest)? (3) is there a special value like "timestamp-optional" and what does it do? (4) can it be set inside packageRules and combined with matchUpdateTypes? Quote the relevant doc text verbatim.

Title: Configuration Options - Mend Renovate CLI Docs
URL: https://docs.renovatebot.com/configuration-options/

(1) **Exact mechanics:**
> When the time passed since the release is *less* than the set `minimumReleaseAge`: Renovate adds a "pending" status check to that update's branch. After enough days have passed: Renovate replaces the "pending" status with a "passing" status check.
> 
> If you use `minimumReleaseAge=3 days`, `prCreation="not-pending"` and `internalChecksFilter="strict"` then Renovate only creates branches when 3 (or more days) have passed since the version was released.
> 
> If you enable `automerge` *and* `minimumReleaseAge`, Renovate Renovate will create PRs immediately, but only automerge them when the `minimumReleaseAge` time-duration has passed. Renovate adds a "renovate/stability-days" pending status check to each branch/PR. This pending check prevents the branch going green to automerge before the time has passed.

(2) **What happens for updates with no release timestamp:**
> If `minimumReleaseAge` is set to a time duration *and* the update has a release timestamp header, then Renovate will check if the set duration has passed. This behavior can be changed using [`minimumReleaseAgeBehaviour`](https://docs.renovatebot.com/configuration-options/#minimumreleaseagebehaviour).
> 
> When set to `timestamp-required`, this version is not treated stable unless there is release timestamp, and that release timestamp is past the [`minimumReleaseAge`](https://docs.renovatebot.com/configuration-options/#minimumreleaseage).
> 
> When set to `timestamp-optional`, Renovate will treat a release without a releaseTimestamp as stable.

(3) **Special value and what it does:**
> Yes, `"timestamp-optional"` is a special allowed value for `minimumReleaseAgeBehaviour`. When set to `timestamp-optional`, Renovate will treat a release without a releaseTimestamp as stable.

(4) **Can it be set inside packageRules and combined with matchUpdateTypes?**
Yes, it can be set inside `packageRules` and combined with `matchUpdateTypes`. Relevant doc text:
> `minimumReleaseAge` is a feature that requires Renovate to wait for a specified amount of time before suggesting a dependency update.
> 
> | Name | Value |
> |---|---|
> | scopes | repo, packageRule, manager, vulnerabilityAlert, updateType |
> | type | string |
> | cli | `--minimum-release-age` |
> | env | `RENOVATE_MINIMUM_RELEASE_AGE` |

In this case, the version `v7` is not updated, but the digest is. When Renovate resolves this update, it looks for the *newest* version matching the current value (which would be the `v7.0.1` version in this case), and then ages the update against the release timestamp for this new version.
[...]
What this means in practice: - On Docker Hub, the release timestamp is the tag's `tag_last_pushed` field, so re-pushing an existing tag restarts the delay and the digest update is held. - Registries which do not return release timestamps (such as GHCR, Quay or ECR) cannot be aged, and the same applies to unversioned tags like `latest`, where no matching version exists to age against. With the default `minimumReleaseAgeBehaviour=timestamp-required`, these digest updates are held indefinitely - configure `minimumReleaseAgeBehaviour=timestamp-optional` to raise them without an age check instead. - Datasources whose timestamps reflect when the matched version was first released (such as `github-tags` for digest-pinned GitHub Actions) cannot detect re-published content. If an existing tag is force-pushed to new commits, the digest update ages against the original release date, so it may pass Minimum Release Age immediately.
[...]
If the current value *does* resolve to a version, but that version's datasource does not expose a release timestamp (for example GHCR, Quay or ECR), the same caveats as `digest` updates apply: the update is held indefinitely under the default `minimumReleaseAgeBehaviour=timestamp-required`, and needs `minimumReleaseAgeBehaviour=timestamp-optional` configured to raise it without an age check.
[...]
Lock file maintenance delegates to the package manager to update package(s), so the updated packages have no release timestamp for Renovate to check. A manager can tell Renovate that its package manager enforces the minimum release age itself while it regenerates the lock file. If you enable `minimumReleaseAgePackageManagerSync`, and the manager does so, then Renovate does not wait for a release timestamp, and the `renovate/stability-days` status check of the lock file maintenance branch passes straight away. Otherwise, lock file maintenance is treated like any other update without a release timestamp. With the default `minimumReleaseAgeBehaviour=timestamp-required`, the `renovate/stability-days` status check stays pending while `minimumReleaseAge` is set. The `security:minimumReleaseAge*` presets set `minimumReleaseAge=null` for lock file maintenance, so these branches are not held back. The minimum release age from the configuration of your package manager does not hold back lock file maintenance on its own, as your package manager applies it itself.
[...]

When the time passed since the release is _less_ than the set `minimumReleaseAge`: Renovate adds a "pending" status check to that update's branch. After enough days have passed: Renovate replaces the "pending" status with a "passing" status check.
[...]
### `minimumReleaseAgeBehaviour=timestamp-optional` warning When Renovate runs with `minimumReleaseAgeBehaviour=timestamp-optional`, Renovate will log a warning, which is then also shown on the Dependency Dashboard. This warning serves to inform users about at least one dependency not being able to adhere to the minimum release age due to the configuration. In cases where this is not desired, you can remap the warning to a lower log level with [`logLevelRemap`](../configuration-options.md#loglevelremap): ```json { "logLevelRemap": [ { "matchMessage": "/Some .+ did not have a releaseTimestamp, but as we're running with minimumReleaseAgeBehaviour=timestamp-optional, proceeding/", "newLogLevel": "info" } ] } ```
[...]
### What happens if the datasource and/or registry does not provide a release timestamp, when using `minimumReleaseAge`? !!! warning Renovate 42 changed the behaviour detailed below. In Renovate 42, the absence of a release timestamp will be treated as if the release is not yet past the timestamp, which provides a safer default. Prior to Renovate 42, we would treat the dependency without a release timestamp **as if it has passed** the `minimumReleaseAge`, and will **immediately suggest that dependency update**. If using Renovate prior you can opt into the more secure behaviour (which is default in Renovate 42) by using [`minimumReleaseAgeBehaviour=timestamp-required`](../configuration-options.md#minimumreleaseagebehaviour) (added in 41.150.0)

Most registries do not expose when a digest itself was published, so to determine the Minimum Release Age cutoff, we age against the release timestamp of the matched _version_. The strength of the guarantee depends on what that timestamp means for your datasource. What this means in practice: - On Docker Hub, the release timestamp is the tag's `tag_last_pushed` field, so re-pushing an existing tag restarts the delay and the digest update is held. - Registries which do not return release timestamps (such as GHCR, Quay or ECR) cannot be aged, and the same applies to unversioned tags like `latest`, where no matching version exists to age against. With the default `minimumReleaseAgeBehaviour=timestamp-required`, these digest updates are held indefinitely - configure `minimumReleaseAgeBehaviour=timestamp-optional` to raise them without an age check instead. - Datasources whose timestamps reflect when the matched version was first released (such as `github-tags` for digest-pinned GitHub Actions) cannot detect re-published content. If an existing tag is force-pushed to new commits, the digest update ages against the original release date, so it may pass Minimum Release Age immediately.
[...]
So, like `digest`, a `pinDigest` update is aged against the release timestamp of the newest version matching the current value, not whatever `currentVersion` resolves to. Unlike `digest` updates, an _unversioned_ current value (such as `latest`) is exempt from `minimumReleaseAge` entirely, rather than being held indefinitely: pinning a reference which already floats to the latest content is strictly safer than leaving it unpinned, so holding it back would only prolong the less-safe, unpinned state. If the current value _does_ resolve to a version, but that version's datasource doesn't expose a release timestamp (for example GHCR, Quay or ECR), the same caveats as [`digest` updates](#digest-updates) apply: the update is held indefinitely under the default `minimumReleaseAgeBehaviour=timestamp-required`, and needs `minimumReleaseAgeBehaviour=timestamp-optional` configured to raise it without an age check.
[...]
#### `lockFileMaintenance` updates Lock file maintenance delegates to the package manager to update package(s), so the updated packages have no release timestamp for Renovate to check. A manager can tell Renovate that its package manager enforces the minimum release age itself while it regenerates the lock file. In that case, Renovate does not wait for a release timestamp, and the `renovate/stability-days` status check of the lock file maintenance branch passes straight away. For all other managers, lock file maintenance is treated like any other update without a release timestamp. With the default `minimumReleaseAgeBehaviour=timestamp-required`, the `renovate/stability-days` status check stays pending while `minimumReleaseAge` is set. The `security:minimumReleaseAge*` presets set `minimumReleaseAge=null` for lock file maintenance, so these branches are not held back.

content.text:
Yes — supported, and it composes cleanly with what we just committed. But the assessment surfaced one thing you should know before deciding: **for `tj-actions` specifically, a release-age gate does not cover the vector that actually burned it in 2025.** Here's the full picture.

## What `minimumReleaseAge` does (verified against Renovate docs)

- It's `packageRule`-scopable and combinable with `matchUpdateTypes`, so a targeted rule is straightforward.
- Mechanics: releases younger than the age get a pending `renovate/stability-days` status check; **automerge is blocked until the age passes**. With the default `prCreation: "immediate"`, the PR itself still appears right away.
- Since Renovate 42, a missing release timestamp means "not yet past the age" (safer default; `timestamp-required`), and `minimumReleaseAgeBehaviour` can override that — we'd leave the default.

**The catch for manual-merge deps:** both named actions are manual in our config (`tj-actions` has explicit `automerge: false`; `retry` sits outside the automerge allowlist). With no branch protection, a human can merge through a pending stability check — so a bare `minimumReleaseAge` would be **cosmetic**: yellow check noise, no actual gate. To make it real, the same rule sets `prCreation: "not-pending"` (verified packageRule-scopable) → the **PR itself is withheld** until the release is ≥ 14 days old, and only then surfaces for your review. Effective worst-case delay is ~21 days, since PR creation also waits for the Monday‑8am scheduled run.

## What it covers — and what it can't

| Vector | Gate effective? |
|---|---|
| Malicious/broken **new release** (v47 → v48.0.0) | ✅ Yes — ages against the GitHub release timestamp; the 2025 payload lived ~3 days before StepSecurity caught it, so a 14‑day soak would very likely have excluded it by review time |
| **Tag repoint without a release** (the actual CVE‑2025‑30066 vector) | ❌ No — docs, verbatim: *"Datasources whose timestamps reflect when the matched version was first released (such as `github-tags` for digest-pinned GitHub Actions) cannot detect re-published content. If an existing tag is force-pushed to new commits, the digest update ages against the original release date, so it may pass Minimum Release Age immediately."* |

For the repoint vector, the controls remain the ones already in place: digest pinning, digest-typed updates staying manual for all actions, and zizmor's online `stale-action-refs`/`impostor-commit` audits running in CI with `GITHUB_TOKEN` (they flag a digest that no longer matches its version comment). One silver lining of `not-pending`: a repoint's digest update ages against the *old* release date, so it passes immediately and **still appears right away** — the gate slows the release vector without blinding you to repoint events.

## Proposed shape (when you say go)

```jsonc
{
  "description": "… soak rationale, repoint caveat, builder exclusion …",
  "matchManagers": ["github-actions"],
  "matchPackageNames": ["tj-actions/changed-files", "nick-fields/retry"],
  "minimumReleaseAge": "14 days",
  "prCreation": "not-pending"
}
```

Two variants to choose between:

- **(a) Soak + manual** (above; keeps the policy we just committed): PRs for these two appear ~2–3 weeks after release, pre-soaked, for human review. Cost: urgent fixes *in* those actions also wait — the bypass is a manual digest bump.
- **(b) Soak + automerge-after-soak**: add `automerge: true` (minor/patch) — this is actually the feature's native sweet spot ("create PRs immediately, but only automerge when the age has passed"). I'd consider it for `retry`; for `tj-actions` I'd still keep manual even soaked, since the repoint vector is unsoakable and it's the one action with a recorded compromise.

Notes: `home-assistant/builder` is the borderline third candidate — org-trusted but publish-path; including it means lagging ≥ 2 weeks behind monthly HA builder releases, so I'd leave it out unless you disagree. Nothing is held today either way: tj-actions v47.0.6 (April), retry v4.0.0 (March), builder 2026.09.0 are all far older than 14 days, so the gate only bites on future releases. And if "higher" implies you're contemplating a global baseline age too — I'd advise against bundling that: it would delay the CI-certified mise tool bumps where green CI already proves correctness, which is exactly what automerge was for.

Say the word and I'll add rule (a) or (b) to the branch.

Hm, I think neither solution is really satisfying. I think I'd like us to not withheld PRs for GH Actions but instead trigger a thorough AI security review for the action bump. We could use Github Copilot for this (my account has 1500 free credits per month), e.g. via an optimized custom `.github/agents/<agent-name>.md` (cf. https://gh.io/customagents and https://gh.io/customagents/config), or maybe GitHub offers some prebuilt feature for this that works reliably (it just needs to be free of cost for my free-tier GitHub account). Please investigate and advise me on how to proceed.

**What are Copilot custom agents (.github/agents/*.md)?**
Custom agents are specialized versions of the Copilot agent tailored to particular tasks and workflows, giving Copilot reusable specialist roles with tailored instructions and tools. - The configuration file's name (minus `.md` or `.agent.md`) is used for deduplication between levels so that the lowest level configuration takes precedence.

YAML frontmatter properties table reference:

| Property | Type | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | string | Display name for the custom agent. Optional. |
| `description` | **Required** string | Description of the custom agent's purpose and capabilities |
| `target` | string | Target environment or context for the custom agent (`vscode` or `github-copilot`). If unset, defaults to both environments. |
| `tools` | list of strings, string | List of tool names the custom agent can use. Supports both a comma separated string and yaml string array. If unset, defaults to all tools. See Tools. |
| `model` | string | Model to use when this custom agent executes. If unset, inherits the default model. |
| `disable-model-invocation` | boolean | Disables Copilot in the cloud from automatically using this custom agent based on task context. When `true`, the agent must be manually selected. Setting `disable-model-invocation: true` is equivalent to `infer: false`. If both are set, `disable-model-invocation` takes precedence. If unset, defaults to `false`. |
| `user-invocable` | boolean | Controls whether this custom agent can be selected by a user. When `false`, the agent cannot be manually selected and can only be accessed programmatically. If unset, defaults to `true`. |
| `infer` | boolean | **Retired**. Use `disable-model-invocation` and `user-invocable` instead. Enables Copilot in the cloud to automatically use this custom agent based on task context. When `false`, the agent must be manually selected. If unset, defaults to `true`. |
| `mcp-servers` | object | Additional MCP servers and tools that should be used by the custom agent. **Not used in VS Code and other IDE custom agents.** |
| `metadata` | object consisting of a name and value pair, both strings | Allows annotation of the agent with useful data. **Not used in VS Code and other IDE custom agents.** |

# Custom agents and sub-agent orchestration Define specialized agents with scoped tools and prompts, then let Copilot orchestrate them as sub-agents within a single session. For dispatching multiple sub-agents in parallel, see [Fleet mode](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-sdk/features/fleet-mode). ## Overview Custom agents are lightweight agent definitions you attach to a session. Each agent has its own system prompt, tool restrictions, and optional MCP servers. When a user's request matches an agent's expertise, the Copilot runtime automatically delegates to that agent as a **sub-agent**—running it in an isolated context while streaming lifecycle events back to the parent session.
[...]
| Concept | Description | |---|---| | **Custom agent** | A named agent config with its own prompt and tool set | | **Sub-agent** | A custom agent invoked by the runtime to handle part of a task | | **Inference** | The runtime's ability to auto-select an agent based on the user's intent | | **Parent session** | The session that spawned the sub-agent; receives all lifecycle events | ## Defining custom agents To discover Markdown definitions from versioned packages or vendored folders, use `agentDirectories` or [Customization discovery locations](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/copilot-sdk/features/customization-locations). Pass `customAgents` when creating a session. Each agent needs at minimum a `name` and `prompt`. TypeScript ```typescript import { CopilotClient } from "@github/copilot-sdk"; const client = new CopilotClient(); await client.start(); const session = await client.createSession({ model: "gpt-5.4", customAgents: [ { name: "researcher", displayName: "Research Agent", description: "Explores codebases and answers questions using read-only tools", tools: ["grep", "glob", "view"], prompt: "You are a research assistant. Analyze code and answer questions. Do not modify any files.", }, { name: "editor", displayName: "Editor Agent", description: "Makes targeted code changes", tools: ["view", "edit", "bash"], prompt: "You are a code editor. Make minimal, surgical changes to files as requested.", }, ], onPermissionRequest: async () => ({ kind: "approve-once" }), }); ```
[...]
In addition to per-agent configuration above, you can set `agent` on the **session config** itself to pre-select which custom agent is active when the session starts. See Selecting an Agent at Session Creation below. | Session Config Property | Type | Description | |---|---|---| | `agent` | `string` | Name of the custom agent to pre-select at session creation. Must match a `name` in `customAgents`. |
[...]
## Selecting an agent at session creation You can pass `agent` in the session config to pre-select which custom agent should be active when the session starts. The value must match the `name` of one of the agents defined in `customAgents`. This is equivalent to calling `session.rpc.agent.select()` after creation, but avoids the extra API call and ensures the agent is active from the very first prompt. TypeScript ```typescript const session = await client.createSession({ customAgents: [ { name: "researcher", prompt: "You are a research assistant. Analyze code and answer questions.", }, { name: "editor", prompt: "You are a code editor. Make minimal, surgical changes.", }, ], agent: "researcher", // Pre-select the researcher agent }); ``` ## How sub-agent delegation works When you send a prompt to a session with custom agents, the runtime evaluates whether to delegate to a sub-agent: 1. **Intent matching**—The runtime analyzes the user's prompt against each agent's `name` and `description` 2. **Agent selection**—If a match is found and `infer` is not `false`, the runtime selects the agent 3. **Isolated execution**—The sub-agent runs with its own prompt and restricted tool set 4. **Event streaming**—Lifecycle events (`subagent.started`, `subagent.completed`, etc.) stream back to the parent session 5. **Result integration**—The sub-agent's output is incorporated into the parent agent's response ### Controlling inference By default, all custom agents are available for automatic selection (`infer: true`). Set `infer: false` to prevent the runtime from auto-selecting an agent—useful for agents you only want invoked through explicit user requests: ```typescript { name: "dangerous-cleanup", description: "Deletes unused files and dead code", tools: ["bash", "edit", "view"], prompt: "You clean up codebases by removing dead code and unused files.", infer: false, // Only invoked when user explicitly asks for this agent }

This policy is enabled by default for organizations with Copilot CLI turned on, but you can confirm or change this setting in your organization's policy settings. 1. See [Managing policies and features for GitHub Copilot in your organization](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/administer-copilot/manage-for-organization/manage-policies). 2. Under "Copilot CLI", confirm that **Allow use of Copilot CLI billed to the organization** is selected. For most automation use cases, we recommend using [GitHub Agentic Workflows](https://github.com/github/gh-aw) rather than invoking `copilot` directly in workflow steps. Agentic workflows use `GITHUB_TOKEN` authentication by default and include additional guardrails suited for automated environments. Your workflow must also grant the `copilot-requests: write` permission. See [Permissions](https://github.github.com/gh-aw/reference/permissions/) in the GitHub Agentic Workflows documentation.

# Running GitHub Copilot CLI programmatically Use Copilot CLI in the terminal, in scripts, or in Actions workflows. ## Introduction You can pass a prompt directly to Copilot CLI in a single command, without entering an interactive session. This allows you to use Copilot directly from the terminal, but also allows you to use the CLI programmatically in scripts, CI/CD pipelines, and automation workflows. To use Copilot CLI programmatically you can do either of the following. - Use the `copilot` command with the `-p` or `--prompt` command-line option, followed by your prompt: Shell ```shell copilot -p "Explain this file: ./complex.ts" ``` - Pipe a prompt to the `copilot` command: Shell ```shell echo "Explain this file: ./complex.ts" | copilot ```
[...]
- **Provide precise prompts** — clear, unambiguous instructions produce better results than vague requests. The more context you give—file names, function names, the exact change—the less guesswork Copilot has to do. - **Quote prompts carefully** — use single quotes around your prompt if you want to avoid shell interpretation of special characters. - **Always give minimal permissions** — use the `--allow-tool=[TOOLS...]` and `--allow-url=[URLs...]` command-line options to give Copilot permission to use only the tools and access that are necessary to complete the task. Avoid using overly permissive options (such as `--allow-all`) unless you are working in a sandbox environment. For more information, see [About local sandboxing for GitHub Copilot](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/about-cloud-and-local-sandboxes). - **Consider `--assisted-approval`** when you can't predict in advance which tools a task will need. A model-based safety review can approve eligible permission requests without you granting blanket permissions. Existing permission rules still apply, and requests that still require your approval are denied in unattended runs. For more information, see [GitHub Copilot CLI programmatic reference](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/reference/copilot-cli-reference/cli-programmatic-reference#using-assisted-permissions). - **Use `-s` (silent)** when capturing output. This suppresses session metadata so you get clean text. - **Use `--no-ask-user`** to turn off the interactive clarifying-question prompt, since there's no user available to respond to it in an automated run. The agent can still ask questions as part of its regular text replies. - **Set a model explicitly** with `--model` for consistent behavior across environments.
